planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring once nighttime lows stay reliably above 40°F, in full sun with sharp drainage; the moderate tree size and thin, easily peeled skin make this one of the better mango cultivars for espalier or large-container culture in marginal zone 9b sites.

directions: Selected in Chiapas, Mexico and now sold commercially as 'Honey' or 'Champagne' mango, Ataulfo produces small, kidney-shaped fruit that ripens to a deep golden yellow with an unusually thin, flattened seed that leaves far more edible flesh per fruit than firmer Florida cultivars like Haden or Kent. The flesh itself is soft, buttery, and virtually fiberless, with an intensely sweet, low-acid, almost custardy flavor and peach-like aroma once fully ripe. Trees are early-to-midseason bearers and stay noticeably more compact and manageable than large seedling-type mangoes, making Ataulfo a good dooryard choice where space is limited.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mango Fruit Facts
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates

common_name: Alphonso Mango (Hapus Mango, Indian Royal Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in spring after all frost danger; give Alphonso a hot, relatively dry ripening period since fruit grown in humid climates is more prone to internal disorders than the Konkan-coast conditions it was selected for.

directions: Widely regarded as India's most prized mango and grown historically along the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, Alphonso bears medium fruit with smooth, deep-orange, fiberless flesh and an intensely fragrant aroma often described as saffron, coconut, and citrus layered together. It is sweeter and less tangy than the Florida-bred commercial cultivars in this collection, but its thin skin and short shelf life make it a specialty dooryard tree rather than a shipping variety outside its native growing region. Fruit ripens mid-season on a vigorous, upright tree, and quality drops noticeably in cooler or more humid climates than its native subtropical range.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Mango Fruit Facts
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant in full sun once all frost danger has passed; because Kensington Pride is polyembryonic, seedling-grown trees will usually come true to type, but grafting still gives the fastest, most reliable route to fruiting.

directions: Australia's leading commercial and backyard mango, Kensington Pride (also called Bowen after its main growing region in Queensland) is valued for a distinctively perfumed, sweet-tangy flavor and vibrant yellow flesh unlike the milder Florida cultivars grown elsewhere in this collection. Fruit is medium to large with yellow-orange skin blushed pink, and unusually for a named cultivar it is polyembryonic, meaning seed-grown trees are typically true clones of the parent. Yields are notably erratic from year to year, and the fruit is softer and more prone to internal breakdown in transit than firmer-fleshed cultivars like Keitt, which is why it remains mostly a domestic Australian variety rather than a major export type.
sources: Mangoes Australia — Kensington Pride Variety Profile
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mango Fruit Facts
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates

common_name: Kesar Mango (Gir Kesar Mango, Queen of Mangoes)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in a hot, relatively dry site; Kesar needs long, warm summers to build the deep sugar content it is known for and performs poorly in cool coastal or heavily overcast climates.

directions: Grown at the foot of Gujarat's Girnar hills and holding Geographical Indication status in India, Kesar is named for its deep saffron-orange, non-fibrous pulp and regularly tests among the sweetest of Indian mango cultivars, often exceeding 22 Brix. Its aroma is rich and rounder than Alphonso, with less tang and a smooth, almost creamy mouthfeel. Fruit is medium-sized and roundish with thin, greenish-yellow, easily peeled skin, ripening on a moderately vigorous tree that needs a long, hot growing season to reach full color and sweetness.
sources: Government of Gujarat — Gir Somnath District Kesar Mango Profile
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mango Fruit Facts
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree only where winters stay frost-free or nearly so, in deep, acidic, well-drained soil; because Bengal bears irregularly, pair it with a more consistent cultivar such as Sweetheart if a dependable annual crop matters more than fruit size.

directions: Bengal produces some of the largest fruit of any lychee cultivar, with bright red, bumpy skin drawn out to a distinct pointed tip and sweet, juicy, mildly floral white flesh with a favorable ratio of flesh to seed. Despite its excellent eating quality, the tree bears irregularly from year to year and has never become a Florida commercial mainstay the way Brewster or Mauritius have, making it more of a connoisseur's dooryard selection than a dependable orchard cultivar. It is grown commercially in parts of Australia and southern Africa and is believed to trace back to a seedling with a West Bengal, India parent.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Lychee Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lychee Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Pine Island Nursery — Litchi chinensis 'Bengal' Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree only where winters stay frost-free or nearly so; because Groff ripens later than most cultivars, hold off harvest until fruit is fully colored and sweet, since it can taste tart if picked while other lychee cultivars would already be ready.

directions: Raised in Hawaii from a Hak Ip seedling and named for horticulturist George Weidman Groff, this late-season cultivar ripens after Brewster and most other lychee in cultivation have already finished, extending the harvest window for growers who have earlier cultivars established. Fruit is smaller than Brewster with dull-red, rough skin and a notably small seed, and the firm white flesh turns sweetly aromatic once it reaches full ripeness, though it can taste acidic if harvested early. Its main value is as a late-ripening companion tree rather than a primary crop.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR — Growing Lychee in Hawaii
California Rare Fruit Growers — Lychee Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lychee Growing in the Florida Home Landscape

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree only where winters stay frost-free or nearly so; the tall, upright growth habit benefits from early structural pruning to keep the canopy within reach for harvest.

directions: One of the oldest and most historically important Chinese lychee cultivars, Kwai Mi forms a tall, upright, vigorous tree that matures a heavy flush of large clusters in May and June, with pink-to-red, bumpy-skinned fruit running around 30 to the pound. The flesh is sweet, fragrant, and juicy with a pleasing balance of crispness and tenderness, though bearing can be inconsistent outside of favorable years. New growth emerges coppery-bronze before turning dark green, and abundant yellow spring flower panicles give it an ornamental character distinct from smoother-leaved cultivars like Mauritius.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR — Growing Lychee in Hawaii
California Rare Fruit Growers — Lychee Fruit Facts
RFCA Archives — Lychee Cultivar Names

common_name: No Mai Tsze Lychee (Glutinous Rice Lychee)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree only where winters stay frost-free or nearly so; expect inconsistent bearing outside an ideal warm, humid subtropical climate, so treat this cultivar as a specialty planting rather than a primary crop tree.

directions: Widely regarded by connoisseurs as the finest-tasting of all lychee cultivars, No Mai Tsze produces intensely crisp, super-sweet flesh around an unusually minute seed, leaving nearly the whole fruit edible. Fruit runs smaller than Brewster or Sweetheart, and the tree's irregular growth habit and inconsistent fruit set outside ideal climates have kept it a rare specialty planting rather than a commercial mainstay. It rewards patient growers willing to trade reliability for exceptional flavor over cultivars bred for consistent yield.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR — Growing Lychee in Hawaii
California Rare Fruit Growers — Lychee Fruit Facts
Pine Island Nursery — Litchi chinensis 'No Mai Tsze' Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in deep, well-drained soil; the compact 8–10 foot mature height makes Golden Pillow one of the few jackfruit cultivars practical for a large container on a patio.

directions: A compact Thai cultivar known locally as Mong Thong, Golden Pillow tops out at only 8 to 10 feet, far more manageable than standard jackfruit trees that can reach 40 to 70 feet. Fruit is also modest for the species at 8 to 10 pounds, with thick, golden, crunchy flesh carrying a mild sweetness and a distinctive musky aftertaste as the fleshy skin spines flatten and separate at ripeness. Its small stature and moderate fruit size make it far better suited to container culture or a small suburban lot than full-sized cultivars like Black Gold or NS1.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jackfruit Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Artocarpus heterophyllus Cultivar Guide
Top Tropicals — Jackfruit 'Golden Pillow' Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in deep, well-drained soil; Honey Gold tolerates regular pruning well and can be kept to roughly 10 by 6 feet without sacrificing fruit set.

directions: Bred as a dwarf selection and popular in both Florida and Australian home orchards, Honey Gold stays dense and prunable, bearing fruit along many lower limbs rather than concentrating it high in the canopy the way standard-sized jackfruit trees do. Fruit is medium at 10 to 12 pounds, with golden-yellow, crisp flesh that is notably sweet and aromatic, closer in texture to Black Gold than to the stringier flesh of unimproved seedling jackfruit. Its manageable size and heavy bearing on young wood have made it a favorite where full-sized cultivars like Black Gold or J-31 would outgrow the available space.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Jackfruit Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Artocarpus heterophyllus Cultivar Guide
Daleys Fruit Tree Nursery — Jackfruit 'Honey Gold' Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger; Reed is a Type A avocado and sets fruit well with a Type B companion such as Fuerte or Sharwil nearby, though it also produces a reliable crop on its own.

directions: Reed is a round, grapefruit-sized Guatemalan-type avocado with thick, pebbled green skin that never darkens, distinguishing it visually from Hass and its black-skinned relatives at a glance. The flesh is exceptionally creamy and buttery, with 18 to 20 percent oil content and a small seed relative to fruit size that leaves an unusually high proportion of edible flesh. It ripens through the heat of summer into early fall, well after spring-ripening cultivars like Fuerte and Zutano have finished, and the tree's narrow, upright form fits smaller yards better than spreading Guatemalan types.
sources: University of California Riverside — Avocado Variety Collection
California Avocado Commission — Reed Avocado Profile
California Rare Fruit Growers — Avocado Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger; Lamb Hass is a Type A avocado that benefits from a Type B companion such as Fuerte or Zutano, and its compact, upright habit suits closer spacing than standard Hass.

directions: A Hass-type seedling selection, Lamb Hass is distinguished by flat, squared shoulders rather than Hass's smoothly curved profile, and by pebbly skin that stays very dark green before darkening further toward black as it fully ripens. Trees grow upright and compact but produce noticeably larger fruit than standard Hass, typically 10 to 18 ounces, and ripen later in the season, extending the black-skinned avocado harvest into early winter after Hass has finished. The rich, smooth, nutty flesh flavor closely echoes Hass itself, making Lamb Hass useful mainly as a season-extending companion rather than a flavor departure.
sources: University of California Riverside — Avocado Variety Collection
California Avocado Commission — Variety Guide
California Rare Fruit Growers — Avocado Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger; Pinkerton is a Type A avocado that blooms and ripens earlier than Hass, so allow extra time after harvest since the fruit softens more slowly than Hass once picked.

directions: Easily identified by its elongated, curved neck and pear shape, Pinkerton is a Guatemalan-leaning Type A avocado with thin, pebbled green skin, a notably small seed, and a high flesh-to-seed ratio that yields more edible fruit per pound than round-fruited cultivars like Reed. It blooms and ripens earlier than Hass, filling the harvest gap from late winter into early summer before mainseason cultivars come on, though the flesh takes noticeably longer to soften after picking. Flavor is creamy and nutty but somewhat milder and less rich than Hass, making it a useful early-season complement rather than a direct substitute.
sources: University of California Riverside — Avocado Variety Collection
California Avocado Commission — Variety Guide
California Rare Fruit Growers — Avocado Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger; Sharwil is a Type B avocado and pairs well with a Type A companion such as Hass or Pinkerton for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: A Guatemalan-Mexican hybrid bred in Australia and now closely associated with Hawaii's Kona coast, Sharwil is unusual for staying green-skinned and bumpy even at full ripeness rather than darkening like Hass or Lamb Hass. Its flesh runs remarkably high in oil, 15 to 25 percent, giving a rich, nutty, almost meaty flavor and an unusually high flesh-to-seed ratio. As a Type B bloomer it ripens through the winter months, filling a harvest window that complements Type A cultivars such as Hass and Pinkerton rather than competing directly with them.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR — Sharwil Avocado Identification
California Avocado Commission — Variety Guide
California Rare Fruit Growers — Avocado Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger; Gwen's naturally compact, slow-growing habit makes it one of the easier avocado cultivars to keep pruned to a manageable dooryard size.

directions: Bred at UC Riverside as a compact, slow-growing descendant of Hass, Gwen stays small enough to prune easily while yielding roughly twice the fruit per acre of standard Hass trees on the same footprint. Fruit is oval and slightly larger than Hass, with thick, pebbled green skin that dulls rather than blackens at ripeness, surrounding creamy gold-green flesh and a small-to-medium seed. Its extended harvest season and naturally compact habit make it useful for growers who want Hass-like flavor without the eventual size of a full standard Hass tree.
sources: University of California Riverside — Avocado Variety Collection
California Avocado Commission — Variety Guide
California Rare Fruit Growers — Avocado Fruit Facts
